title: The reformations, looking back
tomorrow: why does Hebrews call a crowd of runners a cloud?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the middle centuries: a stained-glass window, Francis among the lepers, Julian at her window. Light in dark ages. A new week starts with a boy behind a plow.
screen: `LIGHT IN DARK AGES.` → `A BOY BEHIND A PLOW.`

segments.voice: A group chat in the middle of a fight shows fast who's on which side. Now an older argument. A scholar named William Tyndale is arguing with a learned man about who should be allowed to read the Bible. The story goes that Tyndale ends it with a promise: one day a boy driving a plow will know more scripture than you do. Then he leaves the country to keep it, putting the New Testament into English, in hiding. And the people who don't want it in English are looking for him.
screen: `WHO'S ON WHICH SIDE.` → `TYNDALE'S PLOWBOY PROMISE.` → `ENGLISH, IN HIDING.`

segments.voice: They found him. Tyndale was put to death, and his English kept being read. That's the reformations, plural, because there was more than one, and every one had a cost. Martin Luther, a monk and teacher in Germany, read Paul's letter to the Romans and found a line that turned him around: “The just shall live by faith.” He spoke out against what he saw as abuses in the church, and Protestant churches grew from that break. Menno Simons, a priest in the Netherlands, joined the Anabaptists, who baptized believing adults and would not take up the sword. And inside the Catholic Church, Teresa of Avila was reforming too, founding poorer, simpler convents given to prayer. Looking back honestly, it was also a time of wounds. Christians on more than one side were imprisoned and killed by other Christians, and the family of churches split in ways that still ache. Churches still tell the story differently. Some keep a phrase about themselves: reformed and reforming, never finished being made new. And some churches now pray together, across those old lines, for what Paul asked: “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”
screen: `MORE THAN ONE REFORM.` · `THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.` · `MENNO AND TERESA.` · `A TIME OF WOUNDS.` · then, large: `REFORMED AND REFORMING.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers three people whose church or way is different from yours: a neighbor, a classmate, a relative. For each finger, name one good thing they bring that your own side might miss. If you pray, end with a psalm's line: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
The reformations. Luther, Teresa, Tyndale and Menno: more than one reform, real wounds, and churches still being made new.
Your line: reformed and reforming, never finished being made new. A new week, under way.

howItsDone: Some Protestant churches mark a Reformation Sunday each fall, and some congregations from different churches pray together for Christian unity in a week set aside for it each January.

chat.meaning: The reformations left real wounds. 'Reformed and reforming' means no side is finished; Paul asks for the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Tyndale.meaning: an English scholar who translated the New Testament into English

Anabaptists.meaning: reformers who baptized believing adults and refused the sword

Menno Simons.meaning: a Dutch former priest who led Anabaptists

Teresa of Avila.meaning: a Spanish nun who reformed convents

convents.meaning: communities where nuns live and pray together

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: story). Title, word and carry kept; Romans 1:17, Ephesians 4:3 and Foxe kept. Tyndale's story now carries the hook as an episode; Menno's motto (1 Corinthians 3:11) dropped for length. Psalm 133:1 added to the practice.

Fairness check: Luther 'spoke out against what he saw as abuses'; Catholic reform (Teresa) given equal standing; 'Christians on more than one side were imprisoned and killed'. No dates, numbers or 'ninety-five' theses. Please confirm the balance reads fairly to Catholic, Protestant and Anabaptist readers.

Tyndale's plowboy saying comes from Foxe and is framed as 'the story goes'; paraphrased. 'Put to death' without date, place or charge; 'the people who don't want it in English' names no church. Confirm.

Unity thread (small): the practice counts three people of other churches or ways and ends with Psalm 133:1 (KJV), offered 'if you pray'; 'some churches now pray together, across those old lines' points to the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity (named only in howItsDone).
Grace storyline: three days before the concert the choir splits over the closing song (old hymn vs new arrangement).
Original: Latin 'semper reformanda'; origin and date of the phrase deliberately not claimed.
